questions.q: What are the four sections this lesson recommends for a model card write-up?
options: Introduction, literature review, methodology, references
What this is, how it was trained, results, and limitations
Marketing summary, pricing, FAQ, contact info
Code, comments, tests, changelog
questions.explain: A model card covers what the model is (architecture, data, scope), how it was trained (optimizer, schedule, hardware, duration), the actual results (loss, perplexity, sample quality), and its limitations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the limitations section is the most important one to include, even though it's the easiest to skip?
options: Because it is legally required documentation
Because stating plainly what the model cannot do is what separates an honest write-up from a sales pitch
Because it is the only section readers actually look at
Because PyTorch requires a limitations section in every checkpoint
questions.explain: Overselling capability is the most common failure mode in informal write-ups. Plainly stating what the model cannot do keeps the document credible and useful to someone (including future-you) who wasn't there when it was trained.

questions.q: Why would it be a mistake to claim your Tiny Shakespeare-trained model performs well on general open-domain text?
options: Because perplexity cannot be computed on open-domain text at all
Because the model was trained and evaluated only on a narrow, single-author, character-level corpus, and its results don't transfer to claims about unrelated data
Because open-domain text has no punctuation
Because such a claim would require retraining the tokenizer only
questions.explain: A low perplexity on a small, narrow, single-author corpus says nothing about performance on open-domain text. Claiming otherwise overstates what was actually measured and is exactly the kind of overclaim an honest write-up avoids.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as an honest 'next step' direction after this capstone, without overpromising specific course content?
options: Fine-tuning a pretrained model to adapt it to a narrower task with less data and compute
Immediately deploying the model to serve production traffic
Replacing PyTorch with a different framework entirely
Re-running the exact same capstone with no changes
questions.explain: The lesson names fine-tuning and adaptation, alignment and preference-based training, and scaling laws as the natural next directions -- framed generally, since the guide doesn't claim specifics about courses it hasn't seen.

questions.q: Why does the write-up matter even to the person who trained the model, not just to other readers?
options: It doesn't -- write-ups are only useful for other people, never for yourself
Because details like exact hyperparameters and dataset splits are easy to forget, and a write-up is cheap insurance against that
Because PyTorch deletes checkpoints that lack a written model card
Because write-ups automatically improve a model's perplexity
questions.explain: The lesson notes that three months later, you won't remember your own exact configuration or reasoning. A short write-up is cheap insurance against that, independent of whether anyone else ever reads it.
